title: Authentication and Authorization
summary: Authentication answers who you are; authorization answers what you may do. They are different systems, they fail with different status codes (401 versus 403), and most interview mistakes come from treating them as one word.
analogy: A conference. At the registration desk you show ID and get a badge — that is authentication, and it happens once. At every room door, a steward looks at what is printed on the badge and decides whether this badge opens this room — that is authorization, and it happens every time. The badge is why the system scales: the steward does not phone registration. It is also the weakness: a badge already printed cannot be un-printed, so if one is stolen the only real defences are that it expires soon and that the stewards keep a short list of badges to reject.

explanation.beginner: Authentication is proving who you are — usually by sending a password once. The server must never store that password as you typed it, and must not store it in a form that can be turned back into the password either; it stores a hash, a one-way scramble, deliberately made slow so that guessing is expensive. Once you are recognised, the server gives you something to show on later requests: a session id it remembers, or a signed token it can check without remembering. Authorization is the separate question asked on every request: this is definitely you, but are you allowed to do this? Getting it wrong returns 401 if you did not prove who you are, 403 if you did and still may not.
explanation.interview: Authentication establishes identity; authorization evaluates a policy against that identity, and it is evaluated per request at the resource, not once at login. Credentials are stored as a salted, memory-hard hash (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id) with a per-user random salt, tuned so one verification costs on the order of 100-300 ms — never a fast general-purpose hash like SHA-256, and never encryption, which is reversible by design. Sessions and tokens are a genuine two-sided trade: a server-side session is a lookup per request but revocable instantly; a signed JWT is stateless and needs no lookup but cannot be un-issued, so access tokens are short-lived (minutes) and paired with a long-lived revocable refresh token. A JWT is header.payload.signature, base64url, signed not encrypted — anyone holding it can read the claims, so no secrets in the payload. Validate the algorithm server-side against an allow-list to shut out alg:none and algorithm-confusion mistakes. OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization, OIDC is the identity layer on top of it; for public clients name authorization code with PKCE. For policy, RBAC is simple and auditable, ABAC is expressive and harder to reason about.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.note: Browser or mobile app. Where the token lives here is itself a trade-off: httpOnly cookie plus CSRF defence, or localStorage plus XSS exposure.

nodes.label: Auth service
nodes.note: Verifies credentials once and issues a short-lived access token plus a revocable refresh token.

without: Every service checks the password itself, so the password travels to six places and is hashed six ways — the weakest implementation sets your security
Credentials stored with a fast hash: a leaked table can be attacked at billions of guesses per second on commodity GPU hardware
No single place to disable an account, so revocation means a coordinated change everywhere
with: Credentials are verified in exactly one place, against one slow memory-hard hash with a per-user salt
Downstream services check a signature instead of a password and never see the credential at all
Account disable, password reset and refresh-token revocation are one operation in one system
why.conclusion: Identity is established once, centrally and slowly; it is then presented cheaply everywhere else — which is exactly why the thing presented must expire quickly.

nodes.label: Credential store
nodes.note: Stores salted Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt hashes and nothing reversible. A leak here should cost the attacker real money per guess.

nodes.label: Resource server
nodes.note: Validates the signature and the algorithm, checks expiry, then evaluates policy: 401 if identity failed, 403 if identity succeeded but permission did not.

nodes.label: Session / refresh store
nodes.note: Server-side sessions live here; so do refresh tokens and the deny-list that makes revocation possible before an access token expires.

nodes.label: Protected API
nodes.note: Receives an already-authenticated identity and still authorizes each action against it — authorization is per request, not per login.

without: Passwords stored in plaintext or under a fast hash: one database leak hands the attacker every account, and fast hashes are attackable at billions of guesses per second on ordinary GPU hardware — exactly the property you do not want
Credentials re-sent and re-verified on every request, so the password is on the wire constantly and each verification costs a deliberately slow hash
Every service implements its own permission checks, so the same rule exists in six places and drifts — and the endpoint someone forgot is the one that leaks data
No expiry and no revocation path: a stolen credential is valid until a human notices
with: The password is verified once, in one service, against a salted memory-hard hash that costs the attacker real time per guess
Later requests present a short-lived credential that is cheap to validate and useless after minutes
Policy is evaluated in one well-tested place per request, so a new endpoint inherits the rules instead of inventing them
Revocation exists: sessions can be deleted, refresh tokens invalidated, and the blast radius of a stolen access token is bounded by its lifetime
why.conclusion: Authentication is a one-time expensive proof; authorization is a cheap check repeated on every request. Separating them is what lets a system be both secure and fast — and keeping them separate is what stops 'logged in' from silently meaning 'allowed'.

whenToUse: Any system with user-specific data — which is almost all of them; the question is which mechanism, never whether
Sessions when you control the client and need instant revocation: an admin console, a banking app, anything where 'log this person out now' must mean now
Stateless signed tokens when many independent services must validate identity without a shared lookup on every request
OAuth 2.0 with OIDC when a third party needs access on the user's behalf, or when you want to delegate the password problem to an identity provider entirely
Authorization code with PKCE for any public client — mobile apps and single-page apps, which cannot keep a client secret
whenNotToUse: Do not use a long-lived JWT as a session substitute: it cannot be un-issued, so a token stolen at hour one is valid until it expires, and 'we will just add a deny-list' means you built a session lookup with extra steps and worse ergonomics
Do not roll your own crypto, token format or password hash: the failure is silent, and the standard libraries encode decades of mistakes you would otherwise repeat
Do not put anything confidential in a JWT payload — it is signed, not encrypted, and base64url is encoding, not protection; anyone holding the token reads every claim
Do not use ABAC where RBAC suffices: a policy language nobody can trace becomes a system where no one can answer 'who can read this?', which is an audit failure and usually a security one
Do not authorize at login only — checking permissions once and trusting the session thereafter means a revoked role stays effective until logout, and every new endpoint is unprotected by default

tradeoffs.option: Server-side sessions (opaque session id, state on the server)
pros: Instant revocation: delete the row and the next request is unauthenticated
The identifier carries no data, so nothing leaks if it is read
Session contents can change mid-session — a role change takes effect on the next request
Small cookie, typically tens of bytes
cons: A lookup on every request — cheap in a shared cache (~0.5 ms) but never free, and now on the critical path
The session store is shared state that must be replicated and highly available, or logging everyone out becomes an outage mode
Cross-domain and mobile use is clumsier than a bearer token

tradeoffs.option: Signed tokens / JWT (stateless, verified by signature)
pros: No lookup: validation is a signature check in microseconds, so any service can verify independently
Scales across services and domains without shared session infrastructure
Carries claims (subject, roles, expiry, audience) that services can act on directly
cons: Cannot be un-issued — it is valid until it expires, which forces short lifetimes and a revocation deny-list for the cases that matter
Claims are readable by anyone holding the token, so secrets can never go in the payload
Larger than a session id: hundreds of bytes to ~1 KB on every request
Stale claims: a role revoked now is still asserted until the token expires
Validation mistakes are subtle — accepting alg:none, or letting the token choose the algorithm, turns 'signed' into 'unverified'

tradeoffs.option: Short access token + revocable refresh token (the common compromise)
pros: Fast stateless validation on the hot path, because the access token needs no lookup
Bounded damage: a stolen access token expires in minutes
Revocation is real — invalidate the refresh token and the session cannot be renewed
Refresh-token rotation with reuse detection surfaces theft rather than hiding it
cons: Two credentials, two lifetimes and a refresh flow to implement and get right
A revocation window remains: up to the access token's lifetime
The refresh token is now the crown jewel and needs the strongest storage you have
Clients must handle the mid-request 401-then-refresh-then-retry dance without stampeding

tradeoffs.option: RBAC — permissions attached to named roles
pros: Easy to reason about and easy to audit: 'who can approve refunds?' has a listable answer
Cheap to evaluate and simple to cache
Maps naturally to how organisations already describe jobs
cons: Cannot express context — 'only during business hours', 'only their own department', 'only below £500' all need a new role
Role explosion: combinations multiply until nobody knows what a role means
Per-resource ownership rules fit badly and end up hardcoded next to the role check

tradeoffs.option: ABAC — decisions computed from attributes of user, resource, action and context
pros: Expresses ownership, time, location, data classification and amount limits directly
One policy can replace dozens of roles
Policy can be centralised and changed without redeploying services
cons: Answering 'who can access this?' may require evaluating policy over every user
Evaluation needs attributes at decision time, which means more lookups or a cache that can be stale
Policies become their own hard-to-test codebase, and a subtle rule change can quietly widen access
Debugging a denial is much harder than reading a role list

tradeoffs.option: Browser token storage: httpOnly cookie versus localStorage
pros: httpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie: JavaScript cannot read it, so an XSS bug cannot simply exfiltrate the token, and the browser attaches it automatically
localStorage: no CSRF exposure because nothing is sent automatically, and it works cleanly across domains and for native-style clients
cons: httpOnly cookie: sent automatically, so cross-site request forgery becomes the exposure and you need SameSite plus anti-CSRF tokens on state-changing requests
localStorage: readable by any script on the page, so a single XSS flaw or compromised dependency reads the token directly
Either way the token is only as safe as your content-security policy and dependency hygiene — storage choice moves the risk, it does not remove it

keyNumbers.label: Cost of one password verification, properly tuned
keyNumbers.value: ~100-300 ms of CPU (e.g. bcrypt cost 12, or Argon2id with tens of MiB of memory)

keyNumbers.label: Guess rate against a fast general-purpose hash on commodity GPU hardware
keyNumbers.value: billions per second — which is precisely why fast hashes are the wrong tool

keyNumbers.label: Typical refresh token lifetime
keyNumbers.value: days to weeks, and revocable at any moment

keyNumbers.label: JWT size on every request
keyNumbers.value: a few hundred bytes to ~1 KB, against tens of bytes for an opaque session id

quiz.question: A logged-in user requests an admin-only report and is correctly rejected. Which status code is right, and why?
options: 403 Forbidden — identity was established, the policy denied the action
400 Bad Request — the request was not valid for this user
404 Not Found — never reveal that the endpoint exists
quiz.explanation: 401 means authentication failed or was absent — 'I do not know who you are, try proving it'. 403 means authentication succeeded and authorization failed — 'I know exactly who you are, and you still may not'. The names are historically confusing (401 is literally called 'Unauthorized') which is why candidates mix them up; the distinction that matters is whether identity was established. Returning 404 to hide an endpoint's existence is a deliberate choice some systems make for sensitive resources, but it is a disclosure decision layered on top, not the default correct answer.

quiz.question: Your service issues JWTs valid for 24 hours and validates them statelessly. A user reports their laptop was stolen and asks you to log them out everywhere. Support finds they cannot. What is the underlying problem, and what is the standard fix?
options: The signing key is too weak; rotate to a longer key

A signed token cannot be un-issued — it stays valid until it expires. The standard fix is a short-lived access token (minutes) paired with a long-lived refresh token whose record can be deleted, so revocation bites at the next refresh
The tokens should be encrypted rather than signed
Store the JWT in an httpOnly cookie so the server can delete it
quiz.explanation: This is the defining cost of stateless tokens, and it is the one candidates skip when they call JWTs 'better than sessions'. Validation with no lookup means there is no lookup to change your mind in. Rotating the signing key does work, but it invalidates every user's token at once. Encryption hides the claims and changes nothing about validity. Deleting a cookie only clears the copy in one browser — the thief still has theirs. The real design is a short access token plus a revocable refresh token, ideally with rotation and reuse detection, so the revocation window is bounded by the access token's lifetime rather than a day.

quiz.question: An interviewer asks what OAuth 2.0 is. Which answer is accurate?
options: An authentication protocol that verifies who a user is, replacing passwords

A delegated authorization framework: it lets an application obtain scoped access to resources on a user's behalf. It is not an authentication protocol — OIDC is the identity layer added on top, which returns an ID token describing who the user is
An encryption standard for API traffic
A password hashing specification used by identity providers
quiz.explanation: This is the single most common mix-up in the topic. OAuth 2.0 answers 'may this application act on the user's behalf, and for what scopes?' — it issues access tokens for resources, and deliberately says nothing standard about who the user is. Teams that used it for login had to invent their own identity handling, which is exactly what OpenID Connect standardised: an ID token (a JWT with claims about the user), a userinfo endpoint and a discovery document, layered on the same flows. For public clients that cannot hold a secret — mobile apps and single-page apps — the flow to name is authorization code with PKCE, which binds the code exchange to the client that started it.
